direct_observables: refractive index profile n(x,t) across diffusion zone
schlieren deflection angle proportional to dn/dx
holographic interferometric fringe shift (proportional to integrated refractive index change)
scattered light intensity autocorrelation function g₂(τ) (in DLS mode)
fringe displacement in Mach-Zehnder or Rayleigh interferometry
derived_observables: self-diffusion coefficient (via tracer DLS with labelled particles)
concentration profile c(x,t) from refractive index via dn/dc calibration
hydrodynamic radius R_H (from DLS via Stokes-Einstein relation)
target_properties: mutual diffusion coefficient D₁₂ of binary and ternary liquid mixtures
tracer diffusion coefficient in dilute solutions
intradiffusion (self-diffusion) coefficient via photon correlation spectroscopy
supported_sample_types: supercritical fluid mixtures (with high-pressure optical cell)
unsupported_sample_types: opaque or strongly absorbing liquids (no optical path)
highly turbid or multiple-scattering samples (except backscatter DLS)
solid-state diffusion (no refractive index gradient measurable in situ)
fluorescent samples that interfere with detector (unless filtered)
typical_output_formats: D₁₂ vs. composition at fixed T and P
D₁₂ vs. temperature at fixed composition
concentration profile c(x,t) at successive times
autocorrelation function g₂(τ) vs. delay time (DLS)
D_T and S_T vs. composition or temperature

units.diffusion_coefficient: m²/s (or cm²/s, typically 10⁻⁹ m²/s for liquids)

constraints.hard_limits: limited by optical cell window materials and thermostat capability; specialized cells extend to 200–500 K
constraints.notes: temperature stability of ±0.01 K or better required for accurate diffusion measurements

constraints.hard_limits: high-pressure optical cells can reach 50–100 MPa
constraints.notes: most optical diffusion studies are performed at atmospheric pressure

constraints.hard_limits: must be small enough to ensure Fickian (linear) diffusion regime; must be large enough for detectable refractive index change
constraints.notes: smaller Δc improves linearity but requires higher optical sensitivity

constraints.hard_limits: path length determines fringe sensitivity; too long causes beam distortion from refraction in gradient region
sample must be transparent at the chosen wavelength
constraints.notes: He-Ne 632.8 nm and Ar-ion 488 nm are most common; dn/dλ dispersion must be considered

variables.name: temperature
variables.effect: diffusion coefficient increases with temperature following Arrhenius or Stokes-Einstein behavior

variables.name: composition
variables.typical_values: full mole fraction range 0–1 for binary; selected compositions for multicomponent
variables.effect: D₁₂ is concentration-dependent; measurements at multiple compositions map D₁₂(x)

variables.name: pressure
variables.effect: D₁₂ decreases with increasing pressure due to increased viscosity

variables.name: scattering_angle
variables.effect: determines the scattering wave vector q; D is obtained from the q²-dependence of the decay rate Γ

instrument_components: laser source — He-Ne (632.8 nm), Ar-ion (488/514.5 nm), or diode laser providing coherent, stable illumination

optical diffusion cell — glass or quartz cuvette with flat parallel windows, thermostatted jacket, and sharp initial boundary formation mechanism (sliding plate, capillary injection, or thermal gradient)
beam-shaping optics — spatial filter, collimating lens, and beam expander for uniform illumination of the diffusion zone

interferometer or schlieren/shadowgraph optical train — Mach-Zehnder, Rayleigh, Jamin, or holographic interferometer for gradient visualization; schlieren knife-edge or shadowgraph screen for deflectometric methods
detector — CCD or CMOS camera for imaging fringe patterns or schlieren deflections; photomultiplier tube or avalanche photodiode for DLS
digital correlator (DLS only) — hardware or software autocorrelator computing g₂(τ) from scattered photon arrival times
thermostat — precision water bath or Peltier temperature controller maintaining ±0.01 K stability
goniometer (DLS only) — rotary stage for selecting scattering angle with ±0.1° precision
data acquisition and image analysis system — computer with fringe analysis, curve fitting, or CONTIN/cumulant software
environmental_requirements: vibration-isolated optical table to prevent disturbance of diffusion gradients and optical alignment
temperature-controlled room or enclosure (±1 K) to minimize convective currents near the cell
draft-free environment — air currents can induce parasitic convection in the diffusion cell
darkened room or light-tight enclosure for sensitive photodetection (DLS)
clean environment to minimize dust particles that scatter light and contaminate DLS signals

geometry: rectangular optical cell with flat parallel windows (interferometric and schlieren methods)
sharp initial boundary between solutions of different concentration (free-diffusion methods)
sample_requirements.size_limits: cell volume typically 5–50 mL; DLS requires ~1 mL; diffusion cells typically 20–60 mm tall
sample_requirements.thickness_limits: optical path length 10–50 mm; longer paths increase sensitivity but worsen beam steering
surface_requirements: optically flat windows (λ/10 or better) for interferometric methods
clean, scratch-free interior surfaces to minimize stray light
anti-reflection coated windows reduce parasitic interference fringes
mounting_requirements: rigid mounting on optical table with kinematic positioning
thermal insulation around cell to maintain temperature uniformity
vibration-damped cell holder to prevent convection from mechanical disturbances
preparation_requirements: solutions filtered through 0.2 µm membrane filters to remove dust (critical for DLS)
solutions degassed by sonication or vacuum to prevent bubble formation during measurement
precise gravimetric preparation of solutions at known concentrations (±0.01% mass fraction)
refractive index increment dn/dc measured for the system at the laser wavelength
cell cleaned with chromic acid or plasma treatment and rinsed with filtered solvent

calibration_requirements: measurement of dn/dc (refractive index increment vs. concentration) for the specific system at the operating wavelength and temperature
magnification calibration of imaging system using a precision reticle or known-spacing grid
verification of D₁₂ for a standard binary system (e.g., KCl-water, sucrose-water) to confirm instrument accuracy
thermocouple or thermistor calibration against a certified reference thermometer
scattering-angle calibration using a known particle-size standard (DLS: NIST SRM latex spheres)
correlator time-base calibration using a reference signal
reference_materials: KCl–water system — well-characterized D₁₂ at 298.15 K (Gosting benchmark)
sucrose–water system — NIST reference for mutual diffusion coefficients
NaCl–water system — extensive literature reference data across temperatures
polystyrene latex spheres (NIST SRM 1963a) — DLS calibration standard for angle and correlator
toluene — known Rayleigh ratio and refractive index for DLS absolute calibration
consumables: membrane filters (0.2 µm pore size) for solution filtration
index-matching fluid for cylindrical DLS cells
precision reference solutions for dn/dc measurement
cleaning solvents (chromic acid, acetone, spectro-grade water)
safety_notes: laser safety: appropriate eye protection for the laser wavelength and power class; follow Class 2/3R/3B laser safety protocols
chromic acid cleaning solution is corrosive and a carcinogen — use proper PPE and fume hood
high-pressure optical cells: follow pressure vessel safety guidelines, use proper shielding
organic solvents used in sample preparation require fume hood ventilation

performance.sensitivity: interferometric methods resolve refractive index differences of ~10⁻⁶; DLS detects concentration fluctuations corresponding to D₁₂ down to ~10⁻¹³ m²/s
performance.detection_limit: mutual diffusion coefficients as low as ~10⁻¹² m²/s (DLS); ~10⁻¹⁰ m²/s for interferometric free-diffusion methods

resolution.spatial: interferometric: ~10–50 µm spatial resolution in concentration profile imaging; schlieren: ~100 µm
resolution.temporal: interferometric: fringe capture every 1–60 s; DLS: autocorrelation delay times from 10⁻⁷ s to 10³ s
resolution.spectral: not directly applicable; single laser wavelength typically used

performance.dynamic_range: D₁₂ from ~10⁻¹² m²/s (large macromolecules, DLS) to ~10⁻⁸ m²/s (small molecules in low-viscosity solvents); 4 decades typical
performance.accuracy: 1–5% for D₁₂ depending on the specific optical method: interferometric methods 0.5–2%, schlieren 2–5%, DLS 2–5%
performance.precision: 0.5–2% (repeatability of D₁₂ from replicate measurements under identical conditions)
performance.throughput: single sample system at a time; one diffusion run takes 1–48 hours for free-diffusion methods; DLS measurements take 1–30 minutes per angle
performance.measurement_speed: free-diffusion experiments: 2–48 hours per composition point (slow diffusion requires longer observation); DLS: 5–30 minutes per data point including multi-angle acquisition

data_and_interpretation.raw_signal_type: interferometric: fringe pattern images recording optical path length variations across the diffusion zone; schlieren: deflection angle map proportional to concentration gradient; DLS: photon count time series from which intensity autocorrelation function g₂(τ) is computed
preprocessing_steps: fringe digitization and centroid extraction from interferometric images
conversion of fringe displacement to refractive index profile Δn(x,t) using known fringe spacing
conversion of Δn to concentration profile Δc(x,t) using calibrated dn/dc
baseline subtraction and removal of optical aberration artifacts from fringe data
DLS: baseline correction of autocorrelation function, removal of dust spike artifacts
DLS: normalization of g₂(τ) to obtain field autocorrelation g₁(τ)
analysis_methods: Boltzmann transformation: plot c vs. x/√t — data collapse confirms Fickian diffusion and yields D₁₂ from the slope
Fourier analysis of concentration profiles: D₁₂ extracted from exponential decay rate of each Fourier component
nonlinear least-squares fit of error-function solution c(x,t) = c̄ + (Δc/2)·erf(x/√(4D₁₂t)) to concentration profiles
moment method: compute second moment of concentration profile σ²(t) = 2D₁₂t to extract D₁₂
DLS cumulant analysis: fit ln|g₁(τ)| = -Γτ + (μ₂/2)τ² to obtain mean decay rate Γ = D₁₂q²
DLS CONTIN (constrained regularization): inverse Laplace transform of g₁(τ) to obtain distribution of diffusion coefficients
multicomponent analysis (ternary): eigenvalue decomposition of diffusion coefficient matrix from coupled Fick equations
model_assumptions: Fickian diffusion: flux J = −D₁₂ (dc/dx) with concentration-independent D₁₂ over the small Δc used
one-dimensional diffusion (concentration gradient only along vertical or horizontal axis)
negligible convective transport — density gradients do not induce Rayleigh-Bénard instability
linear relationship between refractive index and concentration over the measurement range (dn/dc = const)
DLS: scattered light is singly scattered (no multiple scattering); Siegert relation g₂(τ) = 1 + β|g₁(τ)|² holds
DLS: translational diffusion dominates decay of g₁(τ) (no rotational or internal mode contributions at low q)
initial boundary is infinitely sharp at t = 0 (free-diffusion methods)
fit_parameters: mean concentration c̄ at the boundary
initial concentration difference Δc (verified against gravimetric preparation)
boundary position x₀ (center of the error function profile)
time offset t₀ (effective start time for imperfect boundary formation)
DLS: decay rate Γ and polydispersity index (PDI) from cumulant fit
ternary systems: four elements of the 2×2 diffusion coefficient matrix D_ij
common_artifacts: convective instability: density inversion across the diffusion boundary causes buoyancy-driven flow, producing asymmetric or distorted concentration profiles
imperfect initial boundary: residual mixing during boundary formation introduces a finite-width initial profile, requiring a time-offset correction in fitting
beam steering: strong refractive index gradients deflect the probe beam, distorting interferometric fringes near the boundary center
vibration-induced convection: mechanical disturbances create parasitic fluid motion that broadens the apparent diffusion profile
DLS dust contamination: large dust particles produce intense, sporadic scattering spikes that corrupt the autocorrelation function
DLS multiple scattering: in concentrated or turbid samples, multiple scattering decorrelates g₁(τ) faster, yielding an overestimated D₁₂
quality_control_checks: Boltzmann scaling test: verify c(x,t) data collapse onto a single curve when plotted as c vs. x/√t
time independence of fitted D₁₂: D₁₂ obtained from successive time intervals should be constant
symmetry check: concentration profile should be symmetric about the boundary center for ideal free diffusion
measure a reference system (KCl-water or sucrose-water) and compare with literature values within ±1%
DLS: verify q²-dependence of Γ by measuring at multiple scattering angles — deviations indicate non-diffusive contributions
DLS: compare cumulant and CONTIN results for consistency; large discrepancies indicate polydispersity or aggregation
repeat measurement at a slightly different Δc to confirm concentration independence of D₁₂
failure_modes: density-driven convection destroying the diffusion profile (wrong orientation of cell or too large Δc)
bubble formation in the cell from dissolved gas, blocking optical path or inducing convection
thermal gradient across the cell inducing Soret-driven flows that contaminate isothermal D₁₂ measurement
laser intensity fluctuations causing fringe contrast variation or DLS baseline drift
cell window contamination (fingerprints, condensation) degrading optical quality and fringe visibility
DLS: detector saturation from excessive scattering (too concentrated sample or dust)

uncertainty.level: typical combined standard uncertainty 1–5% for D₁₂; interferometric methods achieve 0.5–2%, DLS 2–5%
random_sources: thermal noise in the detector (CCD read noise, photomultiplier dark counts)
photon counting statistics in DLS (shot noise)
temperature fluctuations in the thermostat (±0.01–0.05 K)
vibration-induced refractive index fluctuations in the optical path
random pixelation and digitization errors in fringe centroid extraction
systematic_sources: dn/dc calibration uncertainty (typically ±0.5–2% contribution to D₁₂ for interferometric methods)
imperfect initial boundary sharpness (time-offset correction uncertainty)
residual convective transport biasing apparent D₁₂ high
optical aberrations and magnification calibration errors in imaging systems
DLS: scattering-angle calibration uncertainty propagating into q² and thence D₁₂
DLS: refractive index of solvent used to compute q — uncertainty propagates to D₁₂
thermal gradient across the diffusion cell causing Soret contamination of isothermal measurement
concentration dependence of D₁₂ within the ΔC window (D₁₂ is a differential average)
uncertainty.operator_dependence: moderate to high — initial boundary formation technique, cell alignment, cleanliness, and solution filtration quality significantly affect data quality; experienced operators achieve notably better reproducibility
uncertainty.model_dependence: moderate — accuracy depends on validity of Fickian (concentration-independent D₁₂) assumption, one-dimensional transport, and absence of convection; DLS results depend on single-scattering and Siegert relation assumptions
dominant_error_sources: convective contamination (can bias D₁₂ by 5–20% if not eliminated)
DLS: dust contamination and multiple scattering in concentrated samples
reported_as: combined expanded uncertainty U(D₁₂) at 95% confidence (k=2)
relative uncertainty as percentage of D₁₂
comparison with established reference data as accuracy verification

description_block.technique_overview: Optical method is a general category encompassing several optical techniques used to measure diffusion coefficients in liquid mixtures by monitoring spatial and temporal changes in refractive index caused by concentration or temperature gradients. The family includes interferometric methods (Mach-Zehnder, Rayleigh, Jamin, holographic), schlieren and shadowgraph deflectometry, and dynamic light scattering (DLS, also called photon correlation spectroscopy). These techniques exploit the proportionality between refractive index and composition to track the evolution of concentration profiles during free diffusion, or analyze the spontaneous concentration fluctuations at equilibrium (DLS), extracting mutual diffusion coefficients D₁₂ with typical accuracies of 1–5%. The non-contact, non-destructive nature of optical detection makes these methods particularly valuable for fragile or reactive systems.
description_block.how_it_operates: In free-diffusion (interferometric/schlieren) methods, two solutions of slightly different composition are brought into contact across a sharp horizontal boundary inside an optical cell thermostatted to ±0.01 K. As mutual diffusion proceeds, the initially step-like concentration profile evolves into a smooth error-function shape. A laser beam passing through the cell acquires a phase shift proportional to the integrated refractive index along the optical path, producing fringe patterns in an interferometer or deflection signals in a schlieren system. These patterns are recorded by a CCD camera at successive times and digitized to reconstruct the concentration profile c(x,t), from which D₁₂ is extracted by fitting the Fick's law solution. In dynamic light scattering, a focused laser illuminates a small volume of a homogeneous solution at equilibrium, and spontaneous microscopic concentration fluctuations scatter light whose temporal autocorrelation decays exponentially with a rate Γ = D₁₂q², where q is the scattering wave vector determined by the scattering angle.
description_block.core_theory: Free-diffusion methods are grounded in Fick's second law: ∂c/∂t = D₁₂ ∂²c/∂x² for one-dimensional isothermal diffusion with constant D₁₂. For an initial step-function boundary, the analytical solution is c(x,t) = c̄ + (Δc/2)·erf(x/√(4D₁₂t)). The refractive index profile n(x,t) is related to c(x,t) through the refractive index increment dn/dc, which must be independently measured. Interferometric fringe displacement equals Δn·L/λ (where L is the optical path length and λ is the wavelength), providing quantitative access to the concentration profile. For dynamic light scattering, the Siegert relation connects the measured intensity autocorrelation g₂(τ) = 1 + β|g₁(τ)|² to the field autocorrelation g₁(τ) = exp(−Γτ) for a monodisperse diffusing species, where the decay rate Γ = Dq² and q = (4πn/λ)sin(θ/2). In thermal diffusion (Soret effect) measurements, a temperature gradient drives both thermal diffusion (coefficient D_T) and ordinary back-diffusion (D₁₂), reaching steady state when D_T∇T = D₁₂∇c, yielding S_T = D_T/D₁₂.
description_block.setup: A typical interferometric diffusion apparatus consists of a He-Ne or diode laser, beam-expanding and collimating optics, a thermostatted optical diffusion cell with flat parallel quartz windows (20–30 mm path length), and a Mach-Zehnder or Rayleigh interferometer delivering fringe patterns onto a CCD camera. The cell features a sliding plate or capillary injection mechanism for forming a sharp initial boundary between the two solutions. A precision water bath or Peltier controller maintains the cell temperature to ±0.01 K. For schlieren and shadowgraph configurations, a knife edge or screen replaces the interferometer. A DLS setup comprises a focused laser, a cylindrical glass sample cell in an index-matching vat (temperature-controlled), a goniometer-mounted detector (photomultiplier or avalanche photodiode) at selectable scattering angles, and a digital correlator computing the intensity autocorrelation function. All configurations require a vibration-isolated optical table and a draft-free environment.
description_block.suitable_for: Optical methods are broadly suitable for measuring mutual diffusion coefficients in transparent binary and multicomponent liquid mixtures across the full composition range. Interferometric techniques excel for small molecules and electrolyte solutions where high absolute accuracy (0.5–2%) is needed. DLS is uniquely suited for macromolecular and colloidal systems — polymer solutions, protein solutions, micellar and nanoparticle suspensions — where diffusion coefficients are small (10⁻¹² to 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s) and conventional free-diffusion methods would require impractically long observation times. Optical techniques combined with a thermal gradient (thermal diffusion forced Rayleigh scattering, beam deflection, or holographic grating methods) enable measurement of thermal diffusion coefficients D_T and Soret coefficients S_T. These methods are particularly valuable when non-invasive, non-contact measurement is required, and when direct visual observation of the diffusion process provides physical insight.
description_block.core_limitations: All optical methods require that the sample be transparent at the laser wavelength — opaque, strongly colored, or highly turbid solutions cannot be measured (except with specialized backscatter DLS). Free-diffusion interferometric methods require long measurement times (hours to days) for slowly diffusing species, and the initial boundary formation step introduces a systematic uncertainty that must be carefully corrected. Convection due to density instability across the diffusion boundary is a persistent challenge, requiring correct cell orientation (denser solution below) and vibration isolation. The refractive index increment dn/dc must be independently measured, and systems with very small dn/dc yield poor sensitivity. DLS assumes single scattering; concentrated or turbid samples violate this assumption, leading to artifacts. Ternary and higher-order multicomponent systems require more complex analysis (matrix diffusion coefficients) and multiple experimental configurations. Accuracy is generally lower than that of Taylor dispersion or diaphragm cell methods for some systems.
description_block.sample_preparation: Solutions must be prepared gravimetrically with high accuracy (±0.01% in mass fraction) using analytical-grade chemicals and freshly degassed, deionized water or spectroscopic-grade solvents. All solutions are filtered through 0.2 µm membrane filters immediately before use to remove dust particles — this is absolutely critical for DLS and important for interferometric methods to prevent spurious scattering. Solutions are degassed by gentle sonication under partial vacuum or by helium sparging to prevent bubble formation during the measurement. The refractive index increment dn/dc is measured with a differential refractometer at the laser wavelength and measurement temperature. For free-diffusion experiments, the heavier (denser) solution is placed in the lower half of the cell; the lighter solution is carefully layered on top using a syringe or sliding partition to form a sharp boundary with minimal premixing. For DLS, filtered solutions are transferred to scrupulously clean cylindrical cuvettes.
description_block.calibration_and_references: Calibration of an optical diffusion apparatus centers on three elements: (1) optical magnification calibration using a precision reticle or ruled grid placed at the cell plane, establishing the pixel-to-distance conversion for fringe analysis; (2) measurement of the refractive index increment dn/dc with a differential refractometer to an accuracy of ±0.5% or better; and (3) validation of the complete system by measuring D₁₂ for a well-characterized reference system — the KCl–water system at 298.15 K (D₁₂ = 1.994 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s, Gosting laboratory) and the sucrose–water system are widely used benchmarks. For DLS, the scattering angle is calibrated using NIST-traceable latex sphere standards (SRM 1963a, 100 nm diameter) whose known diffusion coefficient yields a check on both the angle calibration and correlator time base. Temperature calibration of the thermometer or thermocouple against an ITS-90 reference is essential, as D₁₂ has a typical temperature coefficient of ~2–3% per kelvin.
description_block.data_interpretation: For interferometric free-diffusion experiments, the raw data are digitized fringe images at successive times from which the refractive index profile Δn(x,t) and hence the concentration profile c(x,t) are reconstructed using the calibrated dn/dc. D₁₂ is extracted by nonlinear least-squares fitting of the error-function solution to the profiles, or equivalently from the slope of the second moment σ²(t) = 2D₁₂t. The Boltzmann similarity transformation — plotting c vs. η = x/√t — provides a visual test of Fickian behavior: all profiles should collapse onto a single master curve. Consistency of D₁₂ across different time windows confirms that convection is absent and the boundary was well-formed. For DLS, the intensity autocorrelation function g₂(τ) is analyzed by cumulant expansion (yielding a mean D₁₂ and polydispersity index) or by constrained regularization (CONTIN) to obtain a distribution of diffusion coefficients. Multi-angle measurements confirm the q²-scaling expected for translational diffusion. Ternary systems require simultaneous fitting of two coupled error-function solutions to extract the four-element diffusion coefficient matrix.
description_block.common_pitfalls: The most critical pitfall in free-diffusion optical methods is convective contamination — if the cell is oriented incorrectly (less dense solution below) or vibrations disturb the fluid, buoyancy-driven flows overwhelm diffusive transport, producing an anomalously large apparent D₁₂. Another frequent error is neglecting the time offset correction for imperfect initial boundary formation: the effective start time of diffusion may differ from the nominal boundary creation time by seconds to minutes, and failing to account for this biases D₁₂ systematically. For DLS, the most common mistake is measuring dusty or inadequately filtered solutions, which produce intense, sporadic scattering events that corrupt the autocorrelation function and yield erratic diffusion coefficients. Using DLS on concentrated or turbid samples without accounting for multiple scattering leads to overestimated D₁₂ values. Poor temperature control (> ±0.05 K fluctuations) introduces scatter comparable to the measurement uncertainty for D₁₂.
description_block.artifacts_and_failure_modes: Convective rolls from density inversion produce highly asymmetric concentration profiles and non-constant D₁₂ values when analyzed at different times — this is the signature diagnostic for convective failure. Beam steering through strong refractive index gradients distorts fringe shapes near the diffusion boundary center, creating apparent deviations from the error-function profile in the central region. Vibration-induced sloshing in the cell generates transient fringe distortions and spurious convective mixing. In DLS, large dust particles produce 'outlier' correlation functions with anomalous long-time tails; these are identified by their irreproducibility between successive acquisitions. Multiple scattering in concentrated samples flattens g₂(τ), reducing the apparent intercept β and shifting the decay rate upward. Laser intensity drift causes gradual baseline changes in both interferometric fringe contrast and DLS correlation function normalization. Bubble formation during measurement blocks the optical path, producing sudden data dropouts (interferometric) or intense static scattering (DLS).
description_block.reporting_checklist: Published optical diffusion results should report: specific optical technique used (interferometric variant, schlieren, DLS), laser wavelength and power, optical cell geometry and path length, thermostat temperature and stability (±K), initial compositions of the two solutions (free diffusion) or solution concentration (DLS), method of initial boundary formation, refractive index increment dn/dc value with wavelength and temperature specified, number of replicate runs, data analysis method (error-function fit, Boltzmann transform, cumulant, CONTIN), scattering angles used (DLS), reference system measurement results for validation, whether D₁₂ reported is at infinite dilution or finite concentration, temperature and pressure at which D₁₂ is reported, combined expanded uncertainty with confidence level (k=2), and any evidence for or against convective contamination. For ThermoML encoding, diffusion coefficients are reported with nCombExpandUncertValue at the 95% confidence level.
